member: Dr. Elena Vasquez — Contact Dynamics and Slip Detection
message:
Slip hold fits inside the grip rating for Dr. Amara Okafor and Prof. Kenji Tanaka.
Plain words: two fingers squeezing a heavy jar need only a firm pinch each when rubber grips well, so the fingertip does not need crushing force to avoid slip. The numbers that decide it are 9.81 N normal per finger to hold 1.00 kg with friction 0.500 in the required normal per finger calculation (E85), about the weight of a 1.00 L milk bottle on each fingertip and therefore everyday pinch, well inside the 50.0 N rating in the BioTac Product Manual (E43) and near 72.8 kPa at 2.00 N grip in the dual-range sweep (E64).

I take up the What is a Track Circuit? (E74) from Dr. Marcus Reid, which states any power loss or broken wire drops the relay to danger.
Plain words: from contact dynamics that fail-safe wiring is the right map for slip, because steady push and slip buzz must travel on separate paths so a dead wire reads as danger not as safe grip. The numbers that decide it are 2200 Hz sampling with 30.0 ms window inside the 43.2 ms gap from 53.6 ms micro-slip to 96.8 ms gross slip in the stick-to-slip transition simulation (E38), where CDC means Capacitance-to-Digital Converter cannot carry 100 to 500 Hz shake at 9.00 ms update in the AD7147A Rev B (E41), so PVDF, where PVDF means Polyvinylidene Fluoride vibration film, must go direct to the MCU, where MCU means Microcontroller Unit, ADC, where ADC means Analog-to-Digital Converter, and the full SPI, where SPI means Serial Peripheral Interface, frame at 51.2 kbit per s in the SPI rate (E52) follows after the 1-bit interrupt.

I take up the How to adjust the sensitivity for AD7147 (E57) from Prof. Kenji Tanaka, which states plus-minus 8.00 pF range with 16-bit steps.
Plain words: from contact dynamics that range rule sets the calibration the grip loop needs, because slip risk is shear over normal against friction and the static path must stay unsaturated while the dynamic path stays separate. The numbers that decide it are 14.6 steps at 1.00 mN in the signal margin counts (E62) rising to 48.9 percent strain at 213 kPa in the dual-range sweep (E64), with trailing-edge stretch and leading-edge squeeze in the Dynamics of fingertip slip (E67) to give direction, about one-tenth of an eye blink for the 30.0 ms decision and therefore fast enough only on the direct path.

Ready, because the 30.0 ms dual-path timing, 9.81 N hold margin and unsaturated static-dynamic split survive my strongest timing and calibration objections, leaving only the named timed-loop bench test with Dr. Marcus Reid.
